Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let $p\in M$,
let $\mathcal E_p\subseteq T_pM$ be the exponential domain and
$\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$ the exponential map of
[[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]], and identify
$T_{h}(T_pM)$ with $T_pM$ by the canonical isomorphism for every
$h\in T_pM$ ([[def-differential-of-a-smooth-map]]).

**(a) The differential in terms of Jacobi fields.** Let $v\in T_pM$, let
$s_1>0$ satisfy $s_1v\in\mathcal E_p$, and let $u\in T_pM$. Let
$\gamma:[0,s_1]\to M$, $\gamma(t):=\exp_p(tv)$ (well defined by star-shapedness
of $\mathcal E_p$), and let $J_u$ be the unique Jacobi field along
$\gamma$ with $J_u(0)=0$ and $D_tJ_u(0)=u$
([[thm-gr-jacobi-equation-and-geodesic-deviation]] clause (c),
[[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]] clause (b)). Then
$$d(\exp_p)_{tv}(tu)=J_u(t)\qquad(0\le t\le s_1);$$
in particular $d(\exp_p)_{s_1v}(s_1u)=J_u(s_1)$ and, in the special case
$s_1=1$, $v\in\mathcal E_p$, $d(\exp_p)_v(u)=J_u(1)$.

**(b) Conjugacy as a kernel condition.** With the notation of (a),
$d(\exp_p)_{s_1v}$ is injective if and only if no nonzero Jacobi field
along $\gamma$ vanishes at $t=0$ and at $t=s_1$. Moreover
$\ker d(\exp_p)_{s_1v}=s_1\{u\in T_pM:J_u(s_1)=0\}$, so
$\dim\ker d(\exp_p)_{s_1v}$ equals the multiplicity of the conjugate
instant $s_1$ whenever $\gamma(s_1)$ is conjugate to $p$ along $\gamma$
([[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]] clause (d)).

**(c) Conjugate instants of a geodesic.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a smooth
geodesic with $\gamma(0)=p$, and let $s_1>0$ with $s_1\in I$ and
$s_1\gamma'(0)\in\mathcal E_p$. Then $\gamma(s_1)$ is conjugate to
$\gamma(0)=p$ along $\gamma$ if and only if $d(\exp_p)_{s_1\gamma'(0)}$ is
not injective.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), let
$a<b$ and let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a smooth future timelike geodesic with
$g(T,T)=-1$, $T:=\gamma'$, such that no instant $s\in(a,b]$ is conjugate to
$a$ along $\gamma$ ([[def-gr-jacobi-field-and-conjugate-instant]]). Let
$N_\gamma$ be the normal bundle of $\gamma$ (clause (e) there) with the
positive definite fibre metric $g$, and for continuous piecewise-$C^1$
normal fields $J,K$ vanishing at $a$ and $b$ define
$$I(J,K):=\int_a^b\Bigl(g(D_sJ,D_sK)+g\bigl(R(T,J)T,K\bigr)\Bigr)ds,$$
the integral being over the smooth pieces of $J$ and $K$; write $I(J):=I(J,J)$
and $|J|:=\sqrt{g(J,J)}$.

**(a) The Jacobi operator on the normal bundle.** For every normal field $J$
the field $C_T(J):=R(T,J)T$ is again normal, and $C_T$ is $g$-selfadjoint on
each fibre: $g(C_T(J),K)=g(J,C_T(K))$ for normal fields $J,K$.

**(b) Matrix form.** Let $E_1,E_2,E_3$ be a parallel $g$-orthonormal frame of
$N_\gamma$ (which exists), and write $J=\sum_iJ^iE_i$, $K=\sum_iK^iE_i$ with
smooth coefficients on the smooth pieces. Then
$g(D_sJ,D_sK)=\sum_i(J^i)'(K^i)'$ and
$g(R(T,J)T,K)=\sum_{i,j}J^jC^i{}_jK^i$ for the smooth symmetric coefficient
functions $C^i{}_j:=g(C_T(E_j),E_i)$, so that the matrix
$C(s)=\bigl(C^i{}_j(s)\bigr)_{i,j}$ is symmetric for every $s$ and
$$I(J,K)=\int_a^b\Bigl(\textstyle\sum_i(J^i)'(K^i)'+J^TCK\Bigr)ds .$$

**(c) Factorization.** Let $A:[a,b]\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be the unique solution
of the initial-value problem
$$A''=CA,\qquad A(a)=0,\qquad A'(a)=I_3 .$$
Then $A(s)$ is invertible for every $s\in(a,b]$, the field
$\Theta(s):=A'(s)A(s)^{-1}$ is symmetric on $(a,b]$ with
$$\Theta'=C-\Theta^2,$$
and for every continuous piecewise-$C^1$ normal field $J$ vanishing at $a$
and $b$,
$$I(J)=\int_a^b\bigl|J'-\Theta J\bigr|^2ds, $$
where $|J'-\Theta J|^2:=\sum_i\bigl((J^i)'-\sum_j\Theta^i{}_jJ^j\bigr)^2$ in
the frame of (b). Consequently $I(J)\ge0$, and $I(J)=0$ if and only if
$J=0$; the index form is positive definite on the space of such fields.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection, whose existence and uniqueness are
supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]; its
Christoffel symbols are the smooth chart functions of
[[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]. Recall that a **geodesic**
is a curve with $D_t\gamma'=0$ in its parameter
([[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]],
[[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]).

**(a) Local existence, uniqueness and maximality.** For every $(p,v)\in TM$
there is a unique maximal geodesic $\gamma_{p,v}:I_{p,v}\to M$ with
$\gamma_{p,v}(0)=p$ and $\gamma_{p,v}'(0)=v$; its domain $I_{p,v}$ is an open
interval containing $0$ and is not asserted to be all of $\mathbb R$.

**(b) Smooth dependence.** The set
$\mathcal G:=\{(t,p,v):t\in I_{p,v}\}\subseteq\mathbb R\times TM$ is open, and
the evaluation map $(t,p,v)\mapsto\gamma_{p,v}(t)$ is smooth on $\mathcal G$.

**(c) Scaling.** For every $s\in\mathbb R$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$,
$t\in I_{p,sv}$ if and only if $st\in I_{p,v}$, and then
$\gamma_{p,sv}(t)=\gamma_{p,v}(st)$.

**(d) The exponential map.** Define $\mathcal E_p:=\{v\in T_pM:1\in I_{p,v}\}$
and $\exp_p:\mathcal E_p\to M$, $\exp_p(v):=\gamma_{p,v}(1)$, and let
$\psi_p:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ be the coordinate isomorphism of a basis
$e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$. Then $\mathcal E_p$ is open and star-shaped about
$0$ (if $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $0\le s\le1$, then $sv\in\mathcal E_p$),
$\exp_p$ is smooth, $\exp_p(0)=p$, and, under the canonical identification
$T_0(T_pM)\cong T_pM$ and the chart $x=\psi_p$ on $T_0M$,
$$d(\exp_p)_0=\operatorname{id}_{T_pM}.$$
Consequently there is a star-shaped open neighborhood $W_p\subseteq\mathcal E_p$
of $0$ such that $\exp_p|_{W_p}$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open subset of
$M$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), whose geodesics
and exponential map are those of [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]].

**(a) Point-normal charts.** For every $p\in M$ there is a smooth chart
$(U,x)$ around $p$ with $x(p)=0$ such that, in the components of this chart,

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0,\qquad \partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0,\qquad g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}.$$

The construction starts from any chart around $p$ and is finite: no frame field
on $U$ and no global trivialization of $TM$ is used.

**(b) Exponential charts.** For every $p\in M$ and every $g_p$-orthonormal
basis $e_0,\dots,e_3$ of $T_pM$ there is a star-shaped open neighborhood
$W\subseteq T_pM$ of $0$ on which $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open
$U_p\ni p$, and the chart

$$u:=\psi\circ\exp_p^{-1}:U_p\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,$$

where $\psi:T_pM\to\mathbb R^4$ is the coordinate isomorphism of the basis,
satisfies $u(p)=0$ and the same three normal-form identities at $p$ as in (a).
Moreover every geodesic through $p$ has, in the chart $u$, the form
$u(\gamma(t))=(t-t_0)\,k$ for a constant $k\in\mathbb R^4$ whenever
$\gamma(t_0)=p$, $k=\psi(\gamma'(t_0))$, and
$(t-t_0)\gamma'(t_0)\in W$. Thus the portion represented by its radial initial
vector in $W$ is a straight coordinate ray through the origin. This claim is
not made for a later portion of a geodesic that may return to $U_p$ after its
radial initial vector has left $W$. No assertion is made about the second
derivatives of the metric at $p$: the construction is first order and does not
make a neighborhood of $p$ isometric to Minkowski space.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $p\in M$.
Let $W_p\subseteq T_pM$ be a star-shaped open neighborhood of $0$ on which
$\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism onto an open set $U_p:=\exp_p(W_p)$, as supplied
by [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]] and
[[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]; identify
$T_v(T_pM)$ with $T_pM$ for every $v$.

**(a) Gauss lemma.** For every $v\in W_p$ and every $w\in T_pM$,

$$g_{\exp_pv}\bigl(d(\exp_p)_v(v),\,d(\exp_p)_v(w)\bigr)=g_p(v,w).$$

**(b) Radial maximum.** Let $\alpha:[0,1]\to U_p$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike curve with $\alpha(0)=p$, with nonzero future timelike one-sided
tangents, set $q:=\alpha(1)$ and $v_q:=\exp_p^{-1}(q)$. Then

$$L_g(\alpha)\le\sqrt{-g_p(v_q,v_q)},$$

and equality holds if and only if there are $v_0\in W_p$ and a piecewise-$C^1$
strictly increasing surjection $\rho:[0,1]\to[0,\rho(1)]$ with
$v_q=\rho(1)v_0$ and $\alpha(t)=\exp_p(\rho(t)v_0)$ for all $t$; that is,
$\alpha$ is a monotone reparametrization of the radial geodesic segment from
$p$ to $q$. Dividing by $c$, the proper-time increment of $\alpha$ is at most
$\frac1c\sqrt{-g_p(v_q,v_q)}$, which is the proper-time increment of that
radial geodesic.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). For $w\in T_pM$ write
$h=h_n$ and $\gamma(w):=-g_p(n,w)$.

1. If $w$ is nonzero future causal, then $\gamma(w)>0$.
2. If $w$ is future unit timelike, then $\gamma(w)\ge1$, with
   $\gamma(w)=1$ if and only if $w=n$, and
   $g_p(h(w),h(w))=\gamma(w)^2-1$.
3. If $w$ is unit timelike, then $w$ is future-directed if and only if
   $g_p(n,w)<0$, and past-directed if and only if $g_p(n,w)>0$; in particular
   $g_p(n,w)\neq0$ for such $w$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$c>0$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

1. **Well-definedness and additivity of proper time.** Let
   $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike worldline
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then the sum defining
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ is the same for every admissible partition of $[a,b]$; it
   is written $\frac1c\int_a^b h$, where $h$ is the piecewise-defined
   proper-time density. For $a<c<b$,
   $\tau(b)-\tau(a)=\bigl(\tau(c)-\tau(a)\bigr)+\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(c)\bigr)$.
   If $a<b$, the increment is strictly positive.

2. **Reparametrization and orientation, including subintervals.** Let
   $a'<b'$ and let $\varphi:[a',b']\to[a,b]$ be $C^1$ up to its included
   endpoints with nonzero derivative everywhere, including one-sided endpoint
   derivatives. Let $\tilde\gamma:=\gamma\circ\varphi$. Its derivative has
   constant sign and $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto its actual image
   interval. If $\varphi'>0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline and
   $$\tilde\tau(b')-\tilde\tau(a')=\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a')).$$
   This equals $\tau(b)-\tau(a)$ when $\varphi(a')=a$ and $\varphi(b')=b$.
   If $\varphi'<0$, then $\tilde\gamma$ is a piecewise-$C^1$ **past** timelike
   traversal. Its unsigned density
   $\tilde h=\sqrt{-g(\tilde\gamma',\tilde\gamma')}$ obeys
   $$\frac1c\int_{a'}^{b'}\tilde h=\tau(\varphi(a'))-\tau(\varphi(b'))>0,$$
   whereas the oriented original difference
   $\tau(\varphi(b'))-\tau(\varphi(a'))$ is negative. For endpoint-reversing
   $\varphi(a')=b$, $\varphi(b')=a$, the latter equals
   $-\bigl(\tau(b)-\tau(a)\bigr)$. This negative oriented difference is not
   elapsed proper time for a future curve; parameter reversal reverses the
   causal direction. Non-surjective maps compare increments over their
   actual image interval, not over the whole original interval.

3. **Proper-time function and four-velocity.** Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a
   $C^1$ future timelike worldline on an interval with nonempty interior and
   let $\tau$ be its proper-time function based at $t_0\in I$
   ([[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]). Then $\tau$ is $C^1$ on
   $I$ with
   $$\tau'(t)=\frac{1}{c}\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}>0,$$
   so $\tau$ is strictly increasing, and at every $t\in I$ the velocity,
   proper-time density and four-velocity satisfy
   $\gamma'(t)=\tau'(t)\,U(t)$ and $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$. If
   $\tau$ is strictly increasing on $I$ with image $J$, then the
   reparametrized curve $\gamma_\tau:=\gamma\circ(\tau|_I)^{-1}$ is a $C^1$
   future timelike worldline on $J$ with
   $$\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)=U\bigl(\tau^{-1}(\sigma)\bigr),\qquad g\bigl(\gamma_\tau'(\sigma),\gamma_\tau'(\sigma)\bigr)=-c^2 .$$
   The same formulas hold piece by piece for a piecewise-$C^1$ future
   timelike worldline, on each open piece and at its endpoints one-sided, with the two
   corner velocities kept distinct.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $c>0$ be a fixed real constant.
All curves below take values in $M$; the physical reading of $c$, of a
worldline as the history of a clock or body, and of the parameter values as
times is not part of this definition and is adopted separately in the
postulates of the framework.

**(a) Regularity classes.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a map. A
**chart representative** of $\gamma$ is the map $x\circ\gamma$ for a smooth
chart $(U,x)$ of $M$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]).

- For $k\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$ and an interior point $t_0\in I$, the map
  $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ at $t_0$** when there is a chart representative
  $x\circ\gamma$ defined near $t_0$ that is $C^k$ there in the componentwise
  Euclidean sense. This condition is independent of the chart: on the overlap
  of two chart representatives the transition map is smooth and the chain rule
  applies ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]],
  [[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]). If $t_0\in I$ is an
  included endpoint of $I$, the coordinate representative and its derivatives through order $k$
  are continuous up to $t_0$ on the relative interval
  $I\cap(t_0-\delta,t_0+\delta)$ for some $\delta>0$, with derivatives at
  $t_0$ taken one-sided. For $k=\infty$ this holds at every finite order.
  Merely possessing a one-sided secant tangent, as defined next, does not
  by itself make a curve $C^1$ at the endpoint. The map $\gamma$ is **$C^k$ on $I$** when it is $C^k$ at
  every point of $I$.

- Let $b\in\mathbb R$ and $\varepsilon>0$. A curve
  $\gamma:(b-\varepsilon,b]\to M$ has **left tangent** $v\in T_{\gamma(b)}M$
  at $b$ when for one — equivalently every — chart $(U,x)$ around
  $\gamma(b)$, writing $v=\sum_{a=0}^{3}v^a\partial_a|_{\gamma(b)}$
  ([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]), the
  difference quotients satisfy
  $\bigl(x^a(\gamma(t))-x^a(\gamma(b))\bigr)/(t-b)\to v^a$ as $t\uparrow b$ for
  $a=0,1,2,3$. A **right tangent** at the left end of a curve is defined
  analogously with $t\downarrow b$. Chart independence is the one-sided
  chain-rule computation for the smooth transition maps
  ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

- A curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ with $a<b$ is **piecewise $C^1$** when there is a
  finite partition $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ such that for every $i$ the
  restriction of $\gamma$ to $[s_{i-1},s_i]$ is $C^1$ up to its included
  endpoints in the one-sided sense above: in every endpoint chart its
  component derivatives on the open piece have continuous one-sided limits,
  agreeing with its endpoint derivatives. Equivalently each piece has a
  $C^1$ extension to its closed parameter piece. In particular its right
  tangent at $s_{i-1}$ and left tangent at $s_i$ exist. Such a
  partition is called **admissible** for $\gamma$. The piece extensions give continuity at the
  corners; no agreement of the
  two one-sided tangents at a corner is required.

**(b) Velocity.** If $\gamma$ is $C^1$ at an interior point $t$, its
**velocity** $\gamma'(t)\in T_{\gamma(t)}M$ is the velocity derivation of
[[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]] translated to the parameter
value $t$. In a chart around $\gamma(t)$ the velocity has the component
expression

$$\gamma'(t)=\sum_{a=0}^{3}\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x^a\circ\gamma\bigr)(t)\,\partial_a|_{\gamma(t)},$$

the coordinate expression of the derivation
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]). At an
included endpoint of the domain, $\gamma'$ means the corresponding one-sided
tangent of clause (a).

**(c) Timelike worldlines.** A **$C^k$ future timelike worldline** is a $C^k$
curve $\gamma:I\to M$ whose velocity $\gamma'(t)$ is future timelike at every
$t\in I$, in the sense of [[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]
and [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]: $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t))<0$
and $g_{\gamma(t)}(\gamma'(t),N_{\gamma(t)})<0$. A **piecewise-$C^1$ future
timelike worldline** is a piecewise-$C^1$ curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ whose
velocity at every point of each open piece and whose one-sided tangents at the
two ends of each piece are future timelike; the definition is applied to a map
on an arbitrary interval $I$ with nonempty interior by requiring it on every
compact subinterval of $I$. A future timelike velocity is in particular
nonzero, so every future timelike worldline is regular.

**(d) Proper time and length.** Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ be a piecewise-$C^1$
future timelike worldline and let $a=s_0<s_1<\cdots<s_m=b$ be an admissible
partition. On each open piece $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ the function

$$h_i(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}\bigl(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s)\bigr)}$$

is continuous and strictly positive: it is a finite sum of products of
continuous real functions in any chart around a point of the piece, as
$g_{ab}\circ\gamma$ and the components of $\gamma'$ are continuous
([[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and the
square root is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ ([[def-rational-power]],
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]). The continuous one-sided limits of the component derivatives, required
by the $C^1$ extension of each piece, and continuity of $g$ imply that
$h_i$ tends to the norm of the corresponding endpoint tangent. The future
timelike hypothesis on those tangents makes these limits strictly positive, and $h_i$ extends to a continuous function on
$[s_{i-1},s_i]$; hence it is Darboux integrable there
([[def-darboux-integral]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]). The
**proper-time increment** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is

$$\tau(b)-\tau(a):=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\int_{s_{i-1}}^{s_i}h_i(s)\,ds,$$

and the **Lorentzian length** of $\gamma$ over $[a,b]$ is
$L_g(\gamma):=c\,(\tau(b)-\tau(a))$. For a base point $s_0\in I$ the
**proper-time function** $\tau:I\to\mathbb R$ of a future timelike worldline is
the function with $\tau(s_0)=0$ and $\tau(s)$ equal to the increment
from $s_0$ to $s$ when $s>s_0$, and minus the increment from $s$ to $s_0$
when $s<s_0$. That the increment is independent of the admissible
partition, so that $\tau$ is well defined, and that it is invariant under
increasing $C^1$ reparametrization are proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]]; the display is the
value for any admissible partition.

**(e) Four-velocity.** Let $\gamma$ be a piecewise-$C^1$ future timelike
worldline and let $t$ be a parameter value at which $\gamma$ is differentiable
(interior point of a piece, or an included endpoint with its one-sided
tangent). The **four-velocity** of $\gamma$ at $t$ is

$$U(t):=\frac{c\,\gamma'(t)}{\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(t)}\bigl(\gamma'(t),\gamma'(t)\bigr)}}\in T_{\gamma(t)}M .$$

By construction $g_{\gamma(t)}(U(t),U(t))=-c^2$, and
$\gamma'(t)=\bigl(\sqrt{-g(\gamma',\gamma')}/c\bigr)U(t)$ with a strictly
positive scalar factor. If $U$ is written as the derivative of $\gamma$ with
respect to proper time, $U=d\gamma/d\tau$, this is a statement proved in
[[lem-gr-proper-time-reparametrization-and-four-velocity]], not part of the
present definition.

**(f) Scope.** Proper time, length and four-velocity are defined only for
future timelike worldlines. A null or spacelike curve receives no proper time
and no four-velocity from this definition, and no limiting or distributional
extension of the square-root integrand to such curves is asserted. The
parametrization of a worldline is part of the data and is arbitrary in this
definition: no affine parameter, no geodesic equation, no completeness or
extendability of the domain, and no measurement or clock reading is assumed.
Null and spacelike regularity classes are not defined here beyond the general
$C^k$ and piecewise-$C^1$ notions of clause (a), which make no causal
requirement.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth and let $p\in M$. The **differential of $F$ at $p$** is the map $dF_p:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ defined by
$$ dF_p(v)([g]):=v([g\circ F]) $$
for every derivation $v\in T_pM$ and every germ $[g]\in C_{F(p)}^\infty(N)$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

**Standing hypothesis for this page.** Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete
ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]),
$\mathbb{N}$ is the set of natural numbers and **contains $0$**
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[def-nat-order]]), $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
is the canonical natural ([[def-canonical-natural]]), and $a, b$ are reals with

$$a \;<\; b .$$

Intervals and their lengths are those of [[def-interval]]; finite sums are those
of [[def-finite-sum]], indexed as $\sum_{i<n}$ over $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

### Partitions

A **partition of $[a,b]$** is a pair $P = (n, t)$ consisting of a natural number
$n \ge 1$ and a sequence $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-sequence]]) with

$$t_0 = a, \qquad t_i < t_{i+1} \ \text{ for every } i < n, \qquad t_k = b \ \text{ for every } k \ge n .$$

The tail convention on the third clause is bookkeeping only: it makes $t$ a
genuine sequence, so that the finite-sum laws of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] apply to
it verbatim, and it costs nothing because no index above $n$ is ever read. The
first two clauses say exactly that

$$a \;=\; t_0 \;<\; t_1 \;<\; \dots \;<\; t_n \;=\; b ,$$

the last equality because $t_n = b$ by the third clause. In particular
$i \mapsto t_i$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on
$\{\, i \in \mathbb{N} : i \le n \,\}$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]),
and $a \le t_i \le b$ for every $i \le n$.

The **point set** of $P$ is the finite set

$$\operatorname{pts}(P) \;:=\; \{\, t_i \ : \ i \le n \,\} \;\subseteq\; [a,b], \qquad a, b \in \operatorname{pts}(P) .$$

The **subintervals** of $P$ are

$$I_i \;:=\; [\,t_i,\ t_{i+1}\,] \qquad (i < n),$$

and their **lengths** are $\Delta_i := t_{i+1} - t_i$. Each $\Delta_i > 0$, so
each $I_i$ is a nondegenerate closed bounded interval ([[def-interval]]). There
are $n$ of them and they are indexed from $i = 0$, not from $i = 1$: the first
subinterval is $[t_0, t_1] = [a, t_1]$.

**The lengths sum to $b - a$.** By the telescoping law, clause 5 of
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]],

$$\sum_{i<n} \Delta_i \;=\; \sum_{i<n} (t_{i+1} - t_i) \;=\; t_n - t_0 \;=\; b - a .$$

**The mesh.** The set $\{\, \Delta_i : i < n \,\}$ is a nonempty finite set of
reals, nonempty because $n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum
([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]). The **mesh** of $P$ is

$$\|P\| \;:=\; \max\{\, \Delta_i \ : \ i < n \,\} \;>\; 0 ,$$

and $\Delta_i \le \|P\|$ for every $i < n$.

**The uniform partition.** For a natural $N \ge 1$, the **uniform partition of
$[a,b]$ into $N$ parts** is $U_N := (N, t)$ with

$$t_i \;:=\; a + \iota(i)\,\frac{b-a}{\iota(N)} \quad (i \le N), \qquad t_k := b \quad (k \ge N).$$

This is a partition: $t_0 = a$; $t_N = a + (b-a) = b$; and $t_{i+1} - t_i =
(b-a)/\iota(N) > 0$ for $i < N$, because $\iota(N) > 0$ and $\iota(i+1) =
\iota(i) + 1$ ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[def-canonical-natural]]). Its
subinterval lengths are all equal to $(b-a)/\iota(N)$, so

$$\|U_N\| \;=\; \frac{b-a}{\iota(N)} .$$

### A partition is determined by its point set

**Claim.** If $P = (n,t)$ and $P' = (n', t')$ are partitions of $[a,b]$ with
$\operatorname{pts}(P) = \operatorname{pts}(P')$, then $n = n'$ and $t_i = t'_i$
for every $i \le n$.

*Proof.* First, $t_i = t'_i$ for every $i \le \min\{n,n'\}$, by induction on $i$
([[thm-induction-principle]]). For $i = 0$ both equal $a$. Suppose $t_j = t'_j$
for all $j \le i$ and $i + 1 \le \min\{n,n'\}$. The set
$S := \{\, x \in \operatorname{pts}(P) : x > t_i \,\}$ has $t_{i+1}$ as its least
element: $t_{i+1} \in S$, and any $x \in S$ is $t_j$ for some $j \le n$ with
$t_j > t_i$, which forces $j > i$ because $t$ is increasing on indices $\le n$,
hence $j \ge i+1$ and $x = t_j \ge t_{i+1}$. The same argument in $P'$ makes
$t'_{i+1}$ the least element of
$\{\, x \in \operatorname{pts}(P') : x > t'_i \,\}$, which is the same set $S$,
since the point sets agree and $t'_i = t_i$. A set has at most one least element
([[def-max-min]]), so $t_{i+1} = t'_{i+1}$.

Second, $n = n'$. If $n < n'$ then $t'_n = t_n = b$ by the previous paragraph,
while $t'_n < t'_{n'} = b$ because $t'$ is increasing on indices $\le n'$ and
$n < n'$; that is impossible. Exchanging the roles of $P$ and $P'$ rules out
$n' < n$. $\square$

So the map $P \mapsto \operatorname{pts}(P)$ is injective, and a partition may be
named by its point set whenever one is exhibited.

### Inserting a point

Let $P = (n,t)$ be a partition of $[a,b]$ and let $c \in [a,b]$. Define a
partition $P + c$ of $[a,b]$ as follows.

- If $c \in \operatorname{pts}(P)$, put $P + c := P$.
- Otherwise $c \ne a$ and $c \ne b$, so $a < c < b$. The set
  $T := \{\, t_i : i \le n \text{ and } t_i < c \,\}$ is a nonempty finite set of
  reals, nonempty because $t_0 = a < c$, so it has a maximum
  ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]]); let $i_0 \le n$ be the unique index with
  $t_{i_0} = \max T$, unique because $t$ is injective on indices $\le n$. Then
  $i_0 < n$, since $t_n = b > c$ puts $t_n \notin T$; and
  $$t_{i_0} \;<\; c \;<\; t_{i_0+1},$$
  the right inequality because $t_{i_0+1} \ne c$ (as $c \notin \operatorname{pts}(P)$)
  and $t_{i_0+1} < c$ would put $t_{i_0+1} \in T$ with $t_{i_0+1} > t_{i_0} = \max T$.
  Put $P + c := (n+1, s)$ with
  $$s_i := t_i \ (i \le i_0), \qquad s_{i_0+1} := c, \qquad s_i := t_{i-1} \ (i_0 + 2 \le i \le n+1), \qquad s_k := b \ (k \ge n+1).$$

In both cases $P + c$ is a partition of $[a,b]$ and

$$\operatorname{pts}(P + c) \;=\; \operatorname{pts}(P) \cup \{c\}, \qquad \|P+c\| \;\le\; \|P\| .$$

The displayed identity is immediate from the two cases. For the mesh: in the
first case nothing changes; in the second the list of subinterval lengths of
$P + c$ is that of $P$ with $\Delta_{i_0}$ replaced by the two numbers
$c - t_{i_0}$ and $t_{i_0+1} - c$, each of which is smaller than
$\Delta_{i_0} = (c - t_{i_0}) + (t_{i_0+1} - c)$ because the other is positive.
So every length of $P + c$ is at most a length of $P$, and the maximum cannot
increase. Finally the index count grows by exactly $1$ in the second case and
not at all in the first.

### Refinement and the common refinement

$P'$ **refines** $P$, and is a **refinement** of $P$, when

$$\operatorname{pts}(P) \;\subseteq\; \operatorname{pts}(P') .$$

Let $P = (n,t)$ and $Q = (m,s)$ be partitions of $[a,b]$. Applying the recursion
theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) to the set $\mathbb{N} \times \mathcal{P}_{[a,b]}$,
where $\mathcal{P}_{[a,b]}$ is the set of partitions of $[a,b]$, with starting
element $(0, P)$ and the map $(j, R) \mapsto (j+1,\ R + s_j)$ — legitimate
because $s_j \in [a,b]$ for every $j \in \mathbb{N}$ — gives a unique family
$(R_j)_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ of partitions with $R_0 = P$ and $R_{j+1} = R_j + s_j$.
The **common refinement** of $P$ and $Q$ is

$$P \vee Q \;:=\; R_{m+1} .$$

**Its point set is the union.** By induction on $j$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]),
$\operatorname{pts}(R_j) = \operatorname{pts}(P) \cup \{\, s_l : l < j \,\}$;
taking $j = m+1$ gives

$$\operatorname{pts}(P \vee Q) \;=\; \operatorname{pts}(P) \cup \operatorname{pts}(Q).$$

Hence $P \vee Q$ refines both $P$ and $Q$; by the uniqueness claim above it is
the **only** partition with that point set, so $P \vee Q = Q \vee P$, and

$$P' \text{ refines } P \quad \Longrightarrow \quad P \vee P' = P' ,$$

since then $\operatorname{pts}(P) \cup \operatorname{pts}(P') =
\operatorname{pts}(P')$.

**Two size bounds, both used later.** Writing $n_R$ for the first component of a
partition $R$:

$$\|P \vee Q\| \;\le\; \|P\|, \qquad n_{P \vee Q} \;\le\; n_P + n_Q - 1 .$$

The first is the mesh bound above applied $m+1$ times. For the second, each
insertion raises the index count by at most $1$, and the two insertions of
$s_0 = a$ and $s_m = b$ raise it by $0$, since $a$ and $b$ already lie in
$\operatorname{pts}(P)$ and hence in $\operatorname{pts}(R_j)$ for every $j$; so
at most $m - 1$ of the $m+1$ insertions increase it.

### The index map of a refinement

Let $P' = (n',t')$ refine $P = (n,t)$. For each $i \le n$ the point $t_i$ lies in
$\operatorname{pts}(P')$, so there is exactly one $\varphi(i) \le n'$ with
$t'_{\varphi(i)} = t_i$, uniqueness because $t'$ is injective on indices $\le n'$.
The resulting map $\varphi$ satisfies

$$\varphi(0) = 0, \qquad \varphi(n) = n', \qquad \varphi(i) < \varphi(i+1) \ \ (i < n),$$

the first two because $t'_0 = a = t_0$ and $t'_{n'} = b = t_n$ together with
injectivity, and the third because $t_i < t_{i+1}$ and $t'$ is increasing on
indices $\le n'$. In particular $n \le n'$. Moreover, for $i < n$ and
$\varphi(i) \le j < \varphi(i+1)$,

$$I'_j \;=\; [\,t'_j,\ t'_{j+1}\,] \;\subseteq\; [\,t_i,\ t_{i+1}\,] \;=\; I_i ,$$

because $t_i = t'_{\varphi(i)} \le t'_j$ and $t'_{j+1} \le t'_{\varphi(i+1)} = t_{i+1}$.

**The blocks are counted by telescoping.** By clause 5 of
[[lem-finite-sum-laws]],
$\sum_{i<n}\big(\varphi(i+1) - \varphi(i)\big) = \varphi(n) - \varphi(0) = n'$,
so, subtracting $\sum_{i<n} 1 = n$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \big(\varphi(i+1) - \varphi(i) - 1\big) \;=\; n' - n ,$$

a sum of $n$ nonnegative integers, one for each block, which vanishes exactly at
the blocks consisting of a single index. This identity is the whole content of
the quantitative bound in [[lem-refinement-inequalities]], and it is also why
$n \le n'$.

Finally, the lengths inside a block sum to the length of the block:

$$\sum_{j = \varphi(i)}^{\varphi(i+1)-1} \Delta'_j \;=\; t'_{\varphi(i+1)} - t'_{\varphi(i)} \;=\; t_{i+1} - t_i \;=\; \Delta_i \qquad (i < n),$$

again by telescoping, applied to the sequence $l \mapsto t'_{\varphi(i)+l}$ and
read through the index-shift convention of [[def-finite-sum]].

derivations.claim: (Invertibility of the exponential differential along the geodesic.) By [L1] and the hypothesis, for every $s\in(0,b]$ there is no nonzero Jacobi field vanishing at $0$ and $s$, so $d(\exp_p)_{sT(0)}$ is injective for every $s\in(0,b]$; at $s=0$ the differential is the identity by [L3] and hence injective. This proves (a), and together with [L2] proves (c).

(Gauss identity throughout the exponential domain.) The identity in [L4] holds at each lift value even if it is outside the small injective normal domain of that supplier's Statement. Indeed fix $v\in\mathcal E_p$ and $w\in T_pM$. Openness and star-shapedness of $\mathcal E_p$ let us form $F(t,r):=\exp_p(t(v+rw))$ for $0\le t\le1$ and all sufficiently small $r$. Put $A:=\partial_tF$ and $J:=\partial_rF$. By [L3], $D_tA=0$ and $g(A,A)=g_p(v+rw,v+rw)$. Torsion freedom gives $D_tJ=D_rA$ by the symmetric coordinate connection formula, and metric compatibility gives [L3, L4, L8, given, algebra]
$$\partial_tg(A,J)=g(A,D_rA)=\tfrac12\partial_rg(A,A)=g_p(v+rw,w).$$
Since $J(0,r)=0$, integrating in $t$ and taking $r=0$ yields $g_{\exp_pv}(d(\exp_p)_v(v),d(\exp_p)_v(w))=g_p(v,w)$, with no injectivity hypothesis. The metric compatibility and torsion identities used here are supplied by [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]] and [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]].

(Finite local-inverse data.) For each $s\in[0,b]$, $d(\exp_p)_{sT(0)}$ is invertible, so by [L7] there is an open $D_s\subseteq T_pM$ containing $sT(0)$ such that $\exp_p|_{D_s}$ is a diffeomorphism onto $V_s:=\exp_p(D_s)$. Since $\{sT(0):s\in[0,b]\}$ is compact, finitely many of the sets $D_{s_1},\dots,D_{s_N}$ cover this segment; write $\psi_j:V_j\to D_j$ for the inverse of the diffeomorphism. Because invertibility of $d(\exp_p)$ is an open condition on the base point, we may shrink each $D_j$ (keeping $s_jT(0)$ in it) so that $d(\exp_p)_{v}$ is invertible for every $v\in D_j$; fix such $D_j,V_j,\psi_j$.

(Compatible local inverse branches and the lift.) Refine the fixed chart partition of (b) by a finite partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_M=b$ so that each radial subsegment $\{sT(0):t_{k-1}\le s\le t_k\}$ is contained in one $D_{j(k)}$. Such a refinement exists by compactness and a Lebesgue number for the open cover of the parameter interval induced by the $D_j$. Write $D_k^*:=D_{j(k)}$, $V_k^*:=V_{j(k)}$, and $\psi_k^*:=\psi_{j(k)}$. At a junction $t_k$, the point $z_k:=t_kT(0)$ lies in both $D_k^*$ and $D_{k+1}^*$, and both inverses send $\gamma(t_k)$ to $z_k$. Therefore [step 2.1, L3, L7, given]
$$O_k:=V_k^*\cap V_{k+1}^*\cap(\psi_k^*)^{-1}(D_k^*\cap D_{k+1}^*)\cap(\psi_{k+1}^*)^{-1}(D_k^*\cap D_{k+1}^*)$$
is an open neighborhood of $\gamma(t_k)$. On $O_k$ both inverse values belong to $D_k^*$ and have the same exponential image, so injectivity on $D_k^*$ makes the inverses agree. Choose the tolerance $\delta$ so small that $\alpha([t_{k-1},t_k])\subseteq V_k^*$ for each $k$, and $\alpha(t_k)\in O_k$ at every junction. These requirements follow from $C^0$ closeness in the fixed charts: each reference subsegment is compact in its corresponding open target, each junction lies in its open $O_k$, and there are only finitely many such conditions. Define $v(s):=\psi_k^*(\alpha(s))$ on $[t_{k-1},t_k]$. The definitions agree at junctions, giving a continuous piecewise-$C^1$ lift with $\exp_p(v(s))=\alpha(s)$. Injectivity of the initial and final branches gives $v(0)=0$ and $v(b)=bT(0)$. This construction allows distinct inverse branches at a repeated spacetime event; compatibility is imposed only at adjacent parameter junctions.

(Uniform timelike control of the lift.) On every refined interval the inverse branch and its derivative are continuous near the compact reference image, so the fixed-chart $C^1$ closeness implies uniform closeness of $v$ to $sT(0)$ and, on each smooth piece, of $v'$ to $T(0)$; the chain rule gives $v'=d\psi_k^*{}_{\alpha(s)}(\alpha'(s))$. To control the endpoint $s=0$ uniformly, choose a convex norm ball $B$ about $T(0)$ whose closure is inside the future timelike cone of $T_pM$, and first shrink the tolerance so that $v'(s)\in B$ throughout the initial refined interval, including one-sided values. Since $v(0)=0$, piecewise integration gives $v(s)/s=s^{-1}\int_0^s v'(t)\,dt\in B$ there; hence $v(s)$ is future timelike for every positive $s$ in this interval. On the remaining compact radial subsegment, bounded away from $0$, uniform $C^0$ control keeps $v(s)$ in the open future timelike cone. Thus one tolerance works for all $s\in(0,b]$. Every $v(s)$ lies in its $D_k^*$, so $d(\exp_p)_{v(s)}$ is invertible by step 2.1.

(Length inequality.) Define $R(s):=\sqrt{-g_p(v(s),v(s))}>0$ on $(0,b]$. On each smooth piece, step 1.2 gives $R'=-g_p(v,v')/R=-g_{\alpha}(N,\alpha')$, where $N:=d(\exp_p)_v(v)/R$ and $\alpha'=d(\exp_p)_v(v')$. The radial tangent has constant squared norm $g_p(v,v)=-R^2$ by metric compatibility along its geodesic. It starts future timelike and remains so by continuity of its pairing with the time-orientation field; hence $N$ is a future unit timelike vector. By [L5], $R'\ge\sqrt{-g(\alpha',\alpha')}$. Integrating over the pieces from $\varepsilon>0$ to $b$ and letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, using $R\to0$ and bounded piecewise-continuous length density, gives $L_g(\alpha)\le R(b)=\sqrt{-g_p(bT(0),bT(0))}=b$.

(Equality case.) If equality holds in step 5.1, the continuous nonnegative function $R'-\sqrt{-g(\alpha',\alpha')}$ on each smooth piece has zero integral, so it vanishes identically by [L8], and by the equality case of [L5] the vector $\alpha'(s)$ is a positive multiple of $N(s)$ at every interior parameter value; since $\alpha'=d(\exp_p)_v(v')$ and $N=d(\exp_p)_v(v)/R$, and $d(\exp_p)_{v(s)}$ is injective by step 4.1, $v'(s)$ is a positive multiple of $v(s)$: $v'(s)=\lambda(s)v(s)$ with $\lambda(s)>0$, piecewise continuous.

(Monotone reparametrization.) Under equality, step 6.1 gives $v'=\lambda v$ with $\lambda>0$ on the smooth pieces. Differentiating $R$ gives $R'=\lambda R$, so $(v/R)'=0$ there. Continuity across the finitely many corners makes $v/R$ one constant vector on $(0,b]$, and its terminal value is $v(b)/R(b)=T(0)$. Thus $v(s)=R(s)T(0)$ and $\alpha(s)=\gamma(R(s))$. Put $\rho(s):=R(s)$ for $s>0$ and $\rho(0):=0$. One has $\rho(b)=b$ and $\rho'=\sqrt{-g(\alpha',\alpha')}>0$ on every smooth piece, so $\rho$ is strictly increasing and surjects onto $[0,b]$. At $0$, $v(s)=s\alpha'(0)+o(s)$ and $v'(s)\to\alpha'(0)$ from the initial piece. Consequently $R(s)/s\to\sqrt{-g_p(\alpha'(0),\alpha'(0))}$ and $R'(s)=-g_p(v,v')/R$ has the same limit, proving the required one-sided $C^1$ extension. Hence $\rho$ is piecewise $C^1$ on $[0,b]$ and gives the equality characterization.

(Converse and conclusion.) Conversely, if $\alpha=\gamma\circ\rho$ with $\rho$ a piecewise-$C^1$ strictly increasing surjection of $[0,b]$ onto itself, and $\alpha$ belongs to the comparison class of (b), then $L_g(\alpha)=L_g(\gamma)=b$ by the reparametrization invariance of [L6], so equality holds in the stated sense. Steps 5.1 and 7.1 give the inequality and the forward equality characterization for every $\alpha$ in the chosen neighborhood, and steps 1.1 and 2.1 give (a) and (c); the proof is complete.

boundaries.evidence: The statement quantifies over a finite family of charts covering the compact segment and over nonempty sets of nearby curves; step 3.1's partition exists because gamma([0,b]) is compact and covered by the finite family, so the cover is never empty and finiteness is proved, not assumed.

Step 7.1 divides by r(b) and by lambda in the relation v' = lambda v; the hypotheses b > 0 and v timelike make r(b) > 0 and lambda > 0, so the denominators cannot vanish, and the excluded case r = 0 is exactly a failure of timelikeness.

The case of a single chart in the cover is included: step 2.1 takes the finite local-inverse data chart by chart, and for a segment contained in one chart the construction reduces to that one inverse, with the partition of step 3.1 having a single nondegenerate interval.

A degenerate variation, where the lifted curve's tangent becomes lightlike or the family fails to be an immersion, is excluded by the explicit C^1-delta closeness and future-timelike hypotheses of clause (b) together with step 4.1; the equality case is instead characterized by reparametrization in steps 6.1 and 8.1.

The interval ends 0 and b carry the fixed endpoints alpha(0) = p and alpha(b) = gamma(b); step 5.1 integrates R(s) on (0,b] and step 6.1 uses continuity as s decreases to 0, which is the one-sided boundary analysis the closed interval requires.

boundaries.reason: The proof fixes finitely many charts and one partition (step 3.1) and then chooses no family: every selection is finite or supplied by the cited local-inverse function theorem, so no choice principle is invoked.

boundaries.evidence: The forward direction of clause (a) is step 1.1: absence of conjugate instants relative to 0 makes the exponential differential invertible up to b, by the cited conjugacy characterization.

The reverse direction is also step 1.1: if gamma(s1) is conjugate to p then the differential is not injective, so the equivalence in clause (a) is discharged in both directions before the maximum argument begins.

citations.quote:
Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]) and let $r,s\ge0$ be integers.

**(a) Tensors at a point.** For $p\in M$, the tangent space $T_pM$ is the real
vector space of derivations at $p$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]) and the cotangent space is
its algebraic dual, $T_p^*M=(T_pM)^*$
([[def-cotangent-space-and-cotangent-bundle-as-a-disjoint-union]]). A **type
$(r,s)$ tensor at $p$** is a multilinear map

$$T_p:(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\longrightarrow\mathbb R,$$

in the sense of [[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]:
the first $r$ arguments are covectors and the last $s$ are vectors. In
particular a type $(1,0)$ tensor is a vector, a type $(0,1)$ tensor is a
covector and a type $(0,2)$ tensor is a bilinear form, so the covariant
$2$-tensors of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]] are exactly the
type $(0,2)$ tensors of this definition.

**(b) The tensor bundle and smooth fields.** The **type $(r,s)$ tensor bundle**
$T^r_sM$ is the disjoint union of the fibres $T^r_sM|_p=\operatorname{Mult}((T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s,\mathbb R)$
over $p\in M$ ([[def-type-r-s-tensor-bundle]]); it carries the smooth
vector-bundle structure defined by the tensor-coordinate change rules
([[thm-tensor-transition-laws-define-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]). A **smooth
tensor field of type $(r,s)$** on $M$ is a family $T=(T_p)_{p\in M}$ assigning
to each $p$ a type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$, such that for every smooth chart
$(U,x)$ of the maximal smooth atlas the **component functions**

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}(q):=T_q\bigl(dx^{a_1}|_q,\dots,dx^{a_r}|_q,\ \partial_{b_1}|_q,\dots,\partial_{b_s}|_q\bigr),\qquad q\in U,$$

are $C^\infty$ on $U$; here the coordinate derivations
$\partial_b|_q=\partial/\partial x^b|_q$ form a basis of $T_qM$
([[thm-coordinate-derivations-form-a-basis-of-the-tangent-space]]) and the
coordinate differentials $dx^a|_q$ form the dual basis of $T_q^*M$
([[thm-coordinate-differentials-form-the-dual-cotangent-basis]]). This is
equivalent to $T$ being a smooth section of $T^r_sM$ in the sense of
[[def-smooth-tensor-field]]: the component functions are the frame
coefficients of the section in the local frame induced by the chart. The
smoothness condition is independent of the chosen smooth atlas and the
components in two overlapping charts are related by the transformation law
proved in the lemma on this page; the definition is therefore chart
independent rather than merely chart-wise.

**(c) Index conventions.** Indices are written $a,b,c,\dots$ for components in
a chart, with the Einstein summation convention: a repeated index, once upper
and once lower, is summed over $0,1,2,3$. An upper index is a contravariant
slot in which a covector is evaluated, a lower index a covariant slot in which
a vector is evaluated. Slots are moved between these positions with the
musical isomorphisms $\flat_p,\sharp_p$ of
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]]; for example, lowering the
first slot of a type $(1,1)$ field uses $(g^\flat T)^a{}_b=g_{ac}T^c{}_b$ and
raising uses $g^{ac}$. This is an identification of slots, not a change of the
field into a field of another kind, and it uses the metric nondegeneracy.

**(d) Scope.** The definition is purely local and chart-based; no global
triviality of $T^r_sM$, no global frame and no choice of metric-compatible
fields is assumed or implied. All fields are smooth ($C^\infty$); no
lower-regularity or distributional tensor field is defined here. The smooth
structure of the tangent bundle, and hence of $T^r_sM$
([[thm-tensor-transition-laws-define-a-smooth-vector-bundle]]), inherits the
axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]] recorded with
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]; the component formulation of smoothness
itself makes no choice.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold with
metric-selected connection $\nabla$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]],
[[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]],
[[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]), and let $R$ be
the curvature operator of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]],
with components $R^a{}_{bcd}$ in a chart.

**(a) Tensoriality.** For all smooth functions $f$ on $M$ and smooth vector
fields $X,Y,Z$ on a common domain, $R(X,Y)Z=-R(Y,X)Z$ and
$$R(fX,Y)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,fY)Z=fR(X,Y)Z,\qquad R(X,Y)(fZ)=fR(X,Y)Z .$$
Consequently, for every $p\in M$, the value $R(X,Y)Z|_p$ depends only on
$X_p,Y_p,Z_p$, and $R$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(1,3)$ on $M$ whose
components in every smooth chart are the functions $R^a{}_{bcd}$ of
[[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]] clause (b).

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel
symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]),
$$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$
on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

**(c) Point-normal formula.** If the chart is point-normal at $p$, that is
$g_{ab}(p)=\eta_{ab}$, $\partial_ag_{bc}(p)=0$ and $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(p)=0$
([[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]), then, writing
$g_{ad,bc}:=\partial_b\partial_cg_{ad}$,
$$R_{abcd}(p)=\tfrac12\bigl(g_{ad,bc}+g_{bc,ad}-g_{bd,ac}-g_{ac,bd}\bigr)(p) .$$
Equivalently, $R^a{}_{bcd}(p)=\tfrac12\,g^{ae}(p)\bigl(\partial_b\partial_cg_{ed}
+\partial_e\partial_dg_{bc}-\partial_e\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_b\partial_dg_{ec}\bigr)(p)$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary, so that $M$ is Hausdorff
and second countable and carries a maximal smooth atlas
([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Let $g$ be a smooth covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$
in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]. Then $g$ assigns
to every $p\in M$ a bilinear form $g_p:T_pM\times T_pM\to\mathbb R$
([[def-derivation-at-a-point-and-tangent-space]]).

**(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every
$p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature
$(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has
inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which
the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive
diagonal entries. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** (or
Lorentzian manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$). In a smooth chart $(U,x)$ the
**components** of $g$ are the $C^\infty$ functions
$g_{ab}(q)=g_q(\partial_a|_q,\partial_b|_q)$ of
[[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]], and $g_{ab}=g_{ba}$ by symmetry.
We use indices $a,b,c,d=0,1,2,3$ and the Einstein summation convention, with
components in a chart written as lower-case indexed symbols and equations
between indexed fields understood basis-independently. These conventions are
fixed once for this library and the physical reading of the symbols is recorded
with the framework postulates, separately from this mathematical definition.

**(b) Pointwise causal structure.** For every $p\in M$ the vocabulary of
[[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]] applies to the Lorentz vector
space $(T_pM,g_p)$: a tangent vector $v\in T_pM$ is **timelike** when
$g_p(v,v)<0$, **null** when $v\neq0$ and $g_p(v,v)=0$, **spacelike** when
$g_p(v,v)>0$, and **causal** when it is timelike or null. Every nonzero
$v\in T_pM$ has exactly one causal character. The **timelike set**
$T_p:=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,v)<0\}$ has exactly two connected components, each
nonempty, open, convex and path-connected; each $g_p$-orthonormal basis
$e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ of $T_pM$ satisfies $g_p(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$
for some ordering, so in particular nonzero orthonormal vectors exist at every
point ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]],
[[lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components]]).

**(c) Time orientation.** A **time orientation** of $(M,g)$, also called a
**choice of future cone**, is a smooth vector field $N$ on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]], whose tangent-bundle
smooth structure uses the axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of
[[def-countable-choice]]; this is the only use of that axiom in this
definition) such that

$$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0\qquad\text{for every }p\in M .$$

The function $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N_p)$ is $C^\infty$ because $g$ is a smooth
covariant $2$-tensor field and $N$ a smooth field, so the condition is a
pointwise strict inequality between a smooth function and $0$; since
$g_p(N_p,N_p)<0$ implies $N_p\neq0$, a time orientation is nowhere vanishing.
A **time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold** is a triple $(M,g,N)$
consisting of a smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and a time orientation $N$.

Given a time orientation $N$ and $p\in M$, the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and we
**define** a nonzero causal vector $v\in T_pM$ to be **future-directed** when
$g_p(v,N_p)<0$ and **past-directed** when $g_p(v,N_p)>0$. The classification of
nonzero causal vectors into exactly these two classes, and its agreement with
the two components of the timelike set (the future component is the component
$C_p^+$ containing $N_p$, and the future closed null cone is
$\operatorname{cl}(C_p^+)\setminus\{0\}$), is proved in
[[lem-gr-future-causal-classification-by-a-timelike-field]]; in particular no
nonzero causal $v$ satisfies $g_p(v,N_p)=0$, so the definition is exhaustive and
mutually exclusive. Replacing $N$ by $-N$ reverses every future/past label, and
two time orientations $N,N'$ determine the same future-directed causal vectors
at every point where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)<0$, while they determine opposite ones
where $g_p(N_p,N'_p)>0$, by
[[lem-gr-timelike-fields-define-equal-or-opposite-future-cones]]; that lemma
also shows the sign of $p\mapsto g_p(N_p,N'_p)$ is constant on every connected
component of $M$.

**(d) The inverse metric.** Because $g_p$ is nondegenerate, it induces at each
$p$ an isomorphism $\flat_p:T_pM\to T_p^*M$, $v\mapsto g_p(v,\cdot)$, and an
inverse metric $g_p^{-1}$ on the dual space; the inverse metric, the musical
isomorphisms and the components $g^{ab}$ are defined separately on this page,
where the smoothness of those components is also proved. Neither construction
uses any choice principle beyond the one already recorded in (c).


**(e) Smooth timelike curves and their scalar normalization.** Before using
these quantities in the physical conventions, fix a positive real scaling
parameter $c$ (with no physical meaning or dimension in this mathematical
item). A **smooth future timelike curve** is a smooth map $\gamma:I\to M$
from a nonempty open real interval $I$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-c-r-and-smooth-maps-between-smooth-manifolds]]) whose velocity derivation
$\gamma'(s)\in T_{\gamma(s)}M$
([[def-velocity-derivation-of-a-smooth-curve]]) satisfies
$g(\gamma',\gamma')<0$ and $g(\gamma',N)<0$ at every $s\in I$.
In a chart its components are $d(x^a\circ\gamma)/ds$, $a=0,1,2,3$.
For a supplied base point $s_0\in I$ and additive constant $\tau_0\in\mathbb R$
define

$$h(s):=\sqrt{-g_{\gamma(s)}(\gamma'(s),\gamma'(s))},\qquad \tau(s):=\tau_0+\frac1c\int_{s_0}^{s}h(r)\,dr,\qquad U(s):=\frac{c\gamma'(s)}{h(s)}.$$

The integral is oriented when $s<s_0$. The function $\tau$ is called
**proper time** for this scaling and $U$ the **four-velocity** of the smooth
curve; its increment times $c$ is the Lorentzian length. The well-definedness
proof below shows $\tau'>0$, that $\tau:I\to\tau(I)$ is a smooth
diffeomorphism, and that $U$ is the velocity of $\gamma\circ\tau^{-1}$.
Thus $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and $U$ is future timelike. This introduces the smooth
case before any physical unit reading; the later worldline definition extends
it to its stated $C^k$, endpoint and piecewise-$C^1$ classes. It asserts no
clock coupling, motion law or physical value of $c$.

**Convention and scope.** The physical reading of a smooth time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold as a classical spacetime model, and the domain in which
that reading is adopted, are recorded in the framework postulate
`post-gr-spacetime-and-classical-domain`; the words spacetime and event carry no
mathematical content beyond this definition, and this item asserts no claim
about nature. The dimension $4$ and the absence of boundary are part of the
data; nothing in the definition assumes that $M$ is nonempty or connected, and
no completeness, extendibility or maximality property of $(M,g)$ is asserted.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

derivations.claim: (The quadratic contraction vanishes on all timelike vectors.) Fix indices $a,d$ and put $Q(v):=R_{abcd}v^bv^c$ for $v\in T_pM$. Taking $W$ and $J$ to be basis vectors in the hypothesis gives $R_{abcd}T^bT^c=0$ for every timelike $T$; that is, $Q(T)=0$ for every timelike $T$.

(Extension to all vectors.) Fix $v\in T_pM$ and a timelike $T_0$, which exists by [L1]. By [L3], $\lambda\mapsto Q(v+\lambda T_0)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2$, and by [L5] the argument $v+\lambda T_0$ is timelike for all sufficiently large $|\lambda|$, so by step 1.1 this polynomial has infinitely many roots. By [L4] the polynomial is identically zero, and evaluating at $\lambda=0$ gives $Q(v)=0$. Since $v$ was arbitrary, $Q\equiv0$ for the fixed pair $(a,d)$; as $a,d$ were arbitrary, $R_{abcd}v^bv^c=0$ for all $a,b,c,d$ and all $v\in T_pM$.
